nodes.label: Seed URLs
nodes.summary: The starting list. The crawl follows links outward from here.

nodes.label: URL frontier
nodes.summary: Hands out URLs by priority and per-host politeness. It outgrows memory, so most of it lives on disk. Mercator waits 10× the last download time before contacting a host again.
nodes.details: Best implementation: priority-level FIFO queues feeding back-end FIFO queues (many more than worker threads), with a priority queue deciding when each host is next eligible.

nodes.label: Fetchers (async)
nodes.summary: Download pages with thousands of concurrent connections. Google's 1998 crawlers kept about 300 connections each and used asynchronous I/O with queues between states. Each keeps its own DNS cache.
nodes.details: 1998: over 100 pages per second at peak with four crawlers. Mercator: ~50 million documents per day on four Alpha servers over 17 days.

nodes.label: robots.txt cache
nodes.summary: Fetched before any content. Cached up to 24 hours (RFC 9309). 4xx means unavailable so access is allowed. 5xx or network errors mean assume complete disallow. Mercator's cache: 2^18 entries, LRU.

nodes.label: Link extractor
nodes.summary: Parses the page, derelativizes links into absolute URLs and passes them to the duplicate eliminator.

nodes.label: URL-seen test (DUE)
nodes.summary: Skips URLs already encountered. Mercator stores 8-byte Rabin fingerprints instead of URLs in a hash table, with a disk-backed variant. A Bloom filter is a common alternative, which is not in the cited paper.

nodes.label: Content-seen test
nodes.summary: Detects documents with the same content under a different URL using stored document fingerprints, and drops them.

nodes.label: Repository
nodes.summary: Compressed copies of fetched pages, each with a docID.

nodes.label: Indexer
nodes.summary: Reads the repository and records hits (word, position, font size, capitalisation). Distributes them into barrels, extracts links and anchor text.

nodes.label: Sorter → inverted index
nodes.summary: Re-sorts barrels from docID order to wordID order, producing the inverted index in place, plus a lexicon for the searcher.

nodes.label: Link graph + PageRank
nodes.summary: The links database (docID pairs) feeds an iterative PageRank computation, a probability distribution over pages.
nodes.details: 1998: PageRank for 26 million pages computed in a few hours on a medium workstation.

nodes.label: Index shards
nodes.summary: Each shard holds an inverted index for a slice of documents. Queries fan out to all shards and the top-K are merged. Elasticsearch makes new documents searchable within about a second via refresh.
nodes.details: The near-real-time refresh behaviour is documented by Elastic. Sharding by document and fan-out is the standard design.

nodes.label: Search front end
nodes.summary: Parses the query, looks up terms, scores with text hits plus PageRank and anchor text, and returns the top results.

nodes.label: Searcher
nodes.summary: Sends a keyword query and expects ranked results in milliseconds.

nodes.label: Crawler
nodes.summary: URL frontier, fetchers, robots.txt cache, link extraction and the URL-seen and content-seen tests.
nodes.details: Grouping container: it names the units the sources describe together. The components inside it are listed in the Components view.

nodes.label: Indexing pipeline
nodes.summary: Indexer, sorter and PageRank over the link graph.
nodes.details: Grouping container: it names the units the sources describe together. The components inside it are listed in the Components view.

steps.caption: The crawl starts from seed URLs.
The frontier hands out a URL whose host is ready, waiting about 10× the last download time between hits to one host.
The fetcher consults the cached robots.txt. A 4xx means the crawler may access anything (RFC 9309 says MAY, a permission), and a 5xx or network error means assume complete disallow.
The page is downloaded asynchronously, with DNS answered from the crawler's own cache.
The content-seen test drops duplicates and stores new pages in the repository.
Links are extracted and made absolute.
The URL-seen test skips URLs already encountered, using compact fingerprints.
Only unseen URLs go back to the frontier, so the loop continues.
The indexer reads compressed pages and records hits for every word.
Hits go into barrels, a partially sorted forward index. The sorter re-sorts them by word to make the inverted index.
The inverted index is split across shards.
Links and anchor text feed the links database, which PageRank turns into authority scores.
A user submits a keyword query.
The front end fans the query out to every shard, each looks up posting lists for the terms, and the top results are merged.
Text matches are combined with PageRank and anchor text to rank the results.
